title: National Gallery of Art: Masterpieces
subtitle: Twenty works in which a pen, a clock, a boat or a flower changes the larger picture.
introduction:
Vermeer's writer has paused, but the pen remains ready above the paper. David's Napoleon stands among objects arranged to suggest work continuing late into the night. These details make claims about the people represented, although a painted claim is not the same thing as independent evidence about a life.

This selection from the National Gallery of Art follows the work done by apparently subordinate objects and gestures. Some identify a subject; some organise space; others ask for belief in an image of duty, intimacy or danger. Looking closely means distinguishing those functions. A significant detail need not be a hidden symbol, and a convincing appearance need not be a candid record.
visitNote: These selected holdings span several periods and gallery areas. Check the National Gallery of Art’s current object records for display locations and loans. Leonardo’s portrait is shown from the front; the reverse is a separate painted surface of the same object.

books.title: A Treatise on Painting
books.author: Leonardo da Vinci; translated by John Francis Rigaud
books.note: Leonardo’s notes examine faces, gestures, light and landscape. They give a closer view of the problems behind the first portrait and offer questions to bring to later artists who solved similar problems differently.

works.title: Ginevra de' Benci
works.credit: Leonardo da Vinci, Ginevra de’ Benci (obverse). National Gallery of Art, Washington, DC. Reproduction via Wikimedia Commons (PD-Art). Full-frame proportional resize and JPEG compression to at most 100,000 bytes; no crop or generated content.
works.description: Dense juniper presses close behind Ginevra, while the water and trees beyond her shoulder open a distant space. Leonardo gives the restrained face these two different settings at once. The contrast strengthens its presence without requiring an expressive gesture. Notice how a portrait can acquire depth through the relationship between its surroundings, rather than through an elaborate pose alone.

works.title: A Lady Writing
works.credit: Johannes Vermeer. A Lady Writing. National Gallery of Art, Washington, 1962.10.1. NGA Open Access — unrestricted reuse; compressed study reproduction.
works.description: The woman turns towards the viewer while keeping her pen poised. Vermeer makes the encounter feel like an interruption because the practical arrangement of writing remains intact. Light catches the yellow jacket against the dark wall, but it is the retained connection to the page that gives the pose its timing. Nothing establishes how long the pause will last.

works.title: Woman Holding a Balance
works.credit: Johannes Vermeer. Woman Holding a Balance. National Gallery of Art. NGA Open Access — public domain. Compressed full-frame reproduction.
works.description: The small balance hangs almost weightlessly above valuables on the table. Behind the woman, the Last Judgment enlarges the question of weighing into one of moral reckoning. Vermeer brings these meanings close without turning each object into a caption for the next. The delicacy of the hand's action remains worth examining even before its possible implications are considered.

works.title: The Annunciation
works.medium: Oil on canvas transferred from panel
works.credit: Jan van Eyck, The Annunciation. National Gallery of Art, Washington, DC. Reproduction via Wikimedia Commons (PD-Art). Full-frame proportional resize and JPEG compression to at most 100,000 bytes; no crop or generated content.
works.description: The angel and Mary occupy a church whose floors, inscriptions and distant architecture carry more information than the two-figure encounter alone. Van Eyck makes close reading part of devotion: small elements connect the announced event with a larger Christian history. The narrow format encourages attention to travel through the building rather than stopping at the figures' exchange.

works.title: Self-Portrait
works.credit: Vincent van Gogh. Self-Portrait. National Gallery of Art. NGA Open Access — public domain. Compressed full-frame reproduction.
works.description: The palette and brushes identify Van Gogh at work, while the strokes around and across his face show the result of that work. Tools and painted handling reinforce one another without becoming identical kinds of evidence. The face remains legible among marks that do not imitate smooth skin. A professional self-image is being constructed through both what is depicted and how it is painted.

works.title: Breezing Up: A Fair Wind
works.credit: Winslow Homer. Breezing Up (A Fair Wind). National Gallery of Art. NGA Open Access — public domain. Compressed full-frame reproduction.
works.description: The boat tilts, and the different positions of the man and boys show them accommodating its movement. Homer gives the apparent pleasure of sailing a practical basis in balance and attention. The choppy water keeps the vessel from becoming a static platform for a group portrait. Their occupation of the boat is inseparable from what the wind is doing to it.

works.title: Watson and the Shark
works.credit: John Singleton Copley. Watson and the Shark. National Gallery of Art. NGA Open Access — public domain. Compressed full-frame reproduction.
works.description: The rescue depends on several actions meeting at the right time: reaching towards the swimmer, positioning the boat and confronting the shark. Copley coordinates those efforts through the men's bodies. The distant waterfront locates the episode but offers no immediate help. Attention remains at the point where a set of separate gestures must become a successful collective act.

works.title: The Skater: William Grant
works.credit: Gilbert Stuart. The Skater (Portrait of William Grant). National Gallery of Art. NGA Open Access — public domain. Compressed full-frame reproduction.
works.description: Grant's crossed arms give the upper body composure, while the angled leg reveals the balance needed below. Stuart adapts the full-length portrait to a skill performed in motion. The distant skaters establish the shared activity without rivaling the principal sitter. The figure's dignity depends on controlled movement, not on the immobility of someone standing for inspection.

works.title: The Voyage of Life: Childhood
works.credit: Thomas Cole. The Voyage of Life: Childhood. National Gallery of Art. NGA Open Access — public domain. Compressed full-frame reproduction.
works.description: The child rides rather than directs the golden boat. Cole turns the river into a route through an allegorical life, with the angel accompanying its beginning. The dark opening behind and the lush, bright world ahead give direction a temporal meaning. A landscape feature does narrative work here: travel across water becomes a way to represent the passage of years.

works.title: The Feast of the Gods
works.artist: Giovanni Bellini, with later landscape alterations by Titian
works.credit: Giovanni Bellini. The Feast of the Gods. Image: WikiArt. Public domain (WikiArt label). Proportionally resized and JPEG compressed; no crop.
works.description: Food, vessels and loosely gathered bodies make the gods' company resemble an outdoor meal. The landscape has its own history of revision: Bellini painted the work in 1514, and Titian reworked its setting in 1529. The apparent unity is therefore the product of more than one moment and one hand, a useful caution against imagining every finished surface as a single decision.

works.title: Laocoön
works.credit: El Greco. Laocoon. WikiArt source label: Public domain. Proportional resize and JPEG compression; no crop. Source: https://www.wikiart.org/en/el-greco/laocoon
works.description: The struggling bodies pull in several directions against the serpents. El Greco places the ancient subject before a city resembling Toledo, refusing the comfortable distance of a conventionally classical setting. Turbulent clouds continue the instability of the limbs above the figures. The threatened balance is not confined to the episode; it becomes a property of the entire painted environment.

works.title: Napoleon in His Study at the Tuileries
works.catalogueTitle: The Emperor Napoleon in His Study at the Tuileries
works.credit: Jacques-Louis David. The Emperor Napoleon in His Study at the Tuileries. National Gallery of Art. NGA Open Access — public domain. Compressed full-frame reproduction.
works.description: Papers, clock and candle are recruited to portray a ruler absorbed in administrative duty. Even the slight disorder of Napoleon's uniform belongs to that carefully constructed account. David does not offer an accidental glimpse into the study. The objects are evidence within the portrait's argument about diligence, not independent proof that the depicted moment happened exactly as shown.

works.title: The Japanese Footbridge
works.credit: Claude Monet. The Japanese Footbridge. National Gallery of Art, Washington, 1992.9.1. NGA Open Access — unrestricted reuse; compressed study reproduction.
works.description: The bridge crosses the upper pond without opening a route to a distant horizon. Monet keeps attention inside the garden, where lily pads, reflected growth and vegetation repeatedly overlap. Depth remains available, but the strokes continually return the eye to the surface. The bridge helps organise that uncertainty by giving the dense field one clearly spanning shape.

works.title: Girl with a Hoop
works.credit: Pierre-Auguste Renoir. Girl with a Hoop. National Gallery of Art, Washington, 1963.10.58. NGA Open Access — unrestricted reuse; compressed study reproduction.
works.description: The hoop connects the girl's hand to the ground and gives her standing pose a possible activity. Renoir does not need to show a game in progress. Broken garden light surrounds a figure who remains sufficiently still to be portrayed. The toy negotiates the difference: she can appear as a particular child outdoors without the image becoming a complete anecdote.

works.title: Self-Portrait
works.credit: Paul Gauguin. Self-Portrait. National Gallery of Art. NGA Open Access — public domain. Compressed full-frame reproduction.
works.description: The halo, snake and apples make competing religious associations cluster around Gauguin's head. Red and yellow fields deny the self-image an ordinary room in which to settle. These signs are acts of self-fashioning rather than straightforward confessions. The painting reveals how the artist chooses to complicate his public image, not an unmediated account of his moral character.

works.title: The Railway
works.credit: Édouard Manet. The Railway. National Gallery of Art. NGA Open Access — public domain. Compressed full-frame reproduction.
works.description: The woman looks out while the child turns towards the railings and steam. Manet divides attention between an encounter offered to the viewer and an activity withheld beyond the bars. The book and dog keep the seated figure occupied in a quieter register. The railway matters through its interruption of visibility; a clearly presented locomotive is unnecessary to the scene.

works.title: Giant Magnolias on a Blue Velvet Cloth
works.catalogueTitle: Giant Magnolias on a Blue Velvet Cloth
works.credit: Martin Johnson Heade. Giant Magnolias on a Blue Velvet Cloth. National Gallery of Art. NGA Open Access — public domain. Compressed full-frame reproduction.
works.description: The magnolias lie on heavy fabric rather than growing in a garden. Heade makes their white petals substantial through the contrast with the deep blue folds. Leaves and dark stems help separate the blossoms while keeping the arrangement close. The change of setting allows flowers to be considered as objects with weight and surfaces, beyond their role in a landscape.

works.title: Little Girl in a Blue Armchair
works.catalogueTitle: Little Girl in a Blue Armchair
works.credit: Mary Cassatt. Little Girl in a Blue Armchair. National Gallery of Art. NGA Open Access — public domain. Compressed full-frame reproduction.
works.description: The child sprawls across furniture large enough to make her temporary occupation of it unmistakable. Cassatt does not correct the body's ungainly ease into a formal portrait pose. Patterned blue upholstery fills much of the room, competing with the small sitter. That imbalance gives childhood a physical measure: adult surroundings continue to exceed the body resting among them.

works.title: The Old Violin
works.credit: John Frederick Peto. The Old Violin. National Gallery of Art. NGA Open Access — public domain. Compressed full-frame reproduction.
works.description: Peto paints wear as carefully as he paints the violin's apparent thickness. Tattered music, marked wood and shadows help flat pigment impersonate separate objects on a door. The deception depends on ordinary evidence of use, not immaculate surfaces. A viewer can know perfectly well that this is a painting and still examine the details that make it look otherwise.

works.title: Jack-in-the-Pulpit No. IV
works.credit: Georgia O'Keeffe. Jack-in-the-Pulpit No. IV. WikiArt source label: Georgia O'Keeffe Fair Use. Proportional resize and JPEG compression; no crop. Source: https://www.wikiart.org/en/georgia-o-keeffe/jack-in-the-pulpit-no-iv
works.license: Georgia O'Keeffe Fair Use (WikiArt source label)
works.description: O'Keeffe enlarges the flower until dark folds and a narrow pale form nearly fill the available space. Curving bands lead towards the central opening, giving botanical structure a scale at which it approaches abstraction. The plant need not disappear for those shapes to acquire independence. Recognition and close attention to colour can remain active together.

closingSections.title: Ask what the detail actually establishes
paragraphs: A pen can establish an activity; a clock can help construct an image of diligence. Neither automatically reveals a private state of mind. Carry that distinction into comparisons between these works. The selection is not a current gallery itinerary; consult museum records for attribution updates, display status and practical visiting information.
